name: Lycopene supplements
short: One pregnancy trial (159 women): more preterm labour and low-birthweight babies on lycopene by mouth than placebo; another: less growth restriction. Case reports: excess lycopene-rich food tints skin.
text: In a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 159 healthy first-time pregnant women, 2 mg of lycopene by mouth daily from 12 to 20 weeks until delivery did not reduce pre-eclampsia (18.18% vs 18.29%), and the lycopene group had significantly more preterm labour (10.39% vs 1.22%) and low-birthweight babies (22.08% vs 9.76%); the authors described these as adverse effects. In contrast, an earlier randomized placebo-controlled trial in 251 first-time pregnant women given oral lycopene until delivery reported less pre-eclampsia (8.6% vs 17.7%) and less intrauterine growth retardation (12% vs 23.7%) with lycopene, and a meta-analysis of oral antioxidant trials in pregnancy (including lycopene) found no benefit for preventing pre-eclampsia. Outside pregnancy, in a 6-month randomized trial in 133 men at increased risk of prostate cancer that included 15 mg lycopene capsules (factorial design with green tea), all interventions were described as acceptable and well tolerated. Case reports describe lycopenaemia, a red-orange or yellow-orange discolouration of the skin (palms, soles) after excessive intake of lycopene-rich fruits and vegetables, described as benign and resolving after dietary change; these reports concern foods, not supplements. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
